definition.text: Conservation finance is raising and managing money to protect land, water and natural resources.

facts.text: It draws on public, private and nonprofit money, using tools from loans and grants to tax breaks and market-based mechanisms, at local to national scales.
Conservation has traditionally been paid for by donations, foundation grants and government money such as tax incentives, ballot measures, bonds and agency budgets.

It is sometimes set apart from fundraising: fundraising gathers money that is never paid back, while conservation finance uses a wider set of financial tools to mobilise and manage capital for conservation results.
Its supporters argue that public and charitable funding falls far short of global needs; one widely cited estimate put yearly needs in the hundreds of billions of dollars, far above actual flows.
To close that gap it tries to add money from financial markets, through debt financing, tax benefits, private equity and project finance.
Early tools were debt-for-nature swaps in the 1980s, followed by incentive-based approaches such as payments for ecosystem services.
By the mid-2000s it was described as a distinct field, and recent analyses stress drawing in private capital through labelled bonds and blended finance.
Deals are usually built around an identifiable source of cash flow or budget authority that can pay for conservation over time.

title: Sources of conservation capital
article: Conservation finance#Sources of capital and actors

definition.text: Money for nature comes from domestic public spending, international public finance including aid, and private spending and investment.

facts.text: Market-rate capital can come from private investors and from public or charitable investors working through development finance institutions and multilateral development banks.
Conservation NGOs and foundations often act as go-betweens that implement projects.
Because NGOs receive much of their income from governments and foundations, adding up total conservation finance risks counting the same money twice.
Public and charitable money is sometimes described as catalytic: covering early costs or sharing risk so that private investment follows.

definition.text: A conservation trust fund is a long-term fund that gives grants to conservation work, often set up as an endowment or a fund spent down over time.

facts.text: They help pay for managing protected areas, including the running costs that short-term grants struggle to cover.
Experience with debt-for-nature swaps helped shape later tools such as conservation trust funds.

definition.text: Three tests of whether paid-for conservation really works: whether the result would not have happened anyway, whether harm simply moves elsewhere, and whether gains last.

facts.text: Additionality asks whether a financed action achieves conservation that would not have happened without the payment.
Leakage, or spillover, is when protecting one place pushes damaging activity to another, cutting the net benefit.

Permanence worries arise where results depend on people keeping to agreements over long periods; durability depends on contract length, enforcement, land pressures and whether behaviour persists after payments stop.
Setting baselines and counterfactuals is hard in practice, which weakens claims of additionality and impact.

definition.text: The costs of finding, assembling, checking, contracting and monitoring conservation projects, often cited as a barrier to scaling up.

facts.text: These costs bite hardest where projects are small, varied or need intensive monitoring and verification.
They can make projects less investable and raise the cost of capital.
Debt-for-nature swaps, for example, need coordination among debtor governments, creditors and NGOs.

title: Measuring conservation finance results

definition.text: Conservation finance deals often require reporting both how money was spent and what ecological results it achieved.

facts.text: Reports may separate outputs, such as area under management, from outcomes, such as changes in ecological condition.
The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures recommends reporting nature-related dependencies and impacts, though data gaps limit consistency.
Payment schemes also raise equity questions: who can be paid, how schemes affect land tenure and livelihoods, and whether wealthier landholders benefit most.

notes: d76a75ba353e names the 'Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)': source mixes TCFD's name with the TNFD acronym; fact text uses TNFD's proper name, verify.

definition.text: Sustainable finance covers the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns.

facts.text: It is often used as a synonym for ESG investing, but the wider field also includes impact investing, social finance and ethical investing.
The Paris Agreement asks parties to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development.
It is described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets.
Green, social and sustainability bonds and sustainability-linked bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025.
Public finance stays important, but much of the money for climate goals is expected to come from the private sector.
Over two decades it grew from a niche topic into a recognised field of research and university teaching.

definition.text: UNEP separates three nested terms often used as synonyms: climate finance, green finance and sustainable finance.

facts.text: Climate finance mainly funds adaptation, resilience, mitigation and a just transition.
Green finance covers climate finance plus other environmental issues such as protecting biodiversity.
Sustainable finance adds social and governance concerns, making it the broadest term for finance that supports sustainable development.
One review traces three periods: forerunners from the 1970s to 2010, an early phase from 2010 to 2021, and a mature phase since 2021.

title: Sustainable finance taxonomy

definition.text: A taxonomy is an official classification that says which economic activities count as green or sustainable for investors.

facts.text: The European Commission set up a technical expert group in 2018 to define such a classification, and the EU taxonomy came into force in July 2020.
Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make greener choices.
Investments are judged against six objectives: climate mitigation, climate adaptation, the circular economy, pollution, water and biodiversity.
Classing fossil gas and nuclear energy as sustainable proved controversial, with some expert advisers threatening to resign over gas.
Mongolia adopted a national green finance taxonomy in 2018, among the first countries to do so.

contested_note: Whether fossil gas and nuclear power belong in the EU taxonomy is disputed.

definition.text: Rules and standards that ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them.

facts.text: The Financial Stability Board launched the Taskforce on Climate-related Financial Disclosures in 2015 to push firms to report climate risks and how they govern them.
Research shows disclosure policies have limited effect when they stay voluntary.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, adopted in October 2022, widens coverage to about 50,000 companies from about 11,700.

title: Green central banking

definition.text: Green central banking is the idea that central banks should use monetary policy and capital rules to help cut emissions and steer money to green investment.

facts.text: In 2018 eight central banks created the Network for Greening the Financial System, which has grown to nearly 116 central banks and supervisors.
Banks have proposed a lighter 'green-supporting factor' on capital rules, while central bankers and nonprofits prefer heavier capital charges on fossil-fuel assets.
Many researchers argue that pursuing such goals strains the legitimacy of independent central banks, whose mandates rarely include climate aims.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether independent central banks may legitimately pursue climate goals.

definition.text: Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting sustainability, so companies and funds are hard to compare.

facts.text: Many bodies write reporting standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors.
One paper found ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time, against 99% for credit ratings from the largest agencies.
This spread is called the ESG ratings gap or 'aggregate confusion'.
Because standards vary and change, some funds labelled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.

title: Economics of biodiversity

definition.text: The economics of biodiversity studies how the variety of life supports the economy and how economic activity in turn harms it.

facts.text: Biodiversity underpins ecosystem services, the benefits people get from ecosystems, and affects how productive ecosystems are.
It supplies food, medicines and industrial materials such as wood, cotton, wool and silk, and supports recreation and tourism.
The WWF Living Planet Report of 2018 argued that the whole global economy, worth US$125 trillion, ultimately relies on nature.
Most species have never been assessed for their present or future economic importance.
Valuing biodiversity mainly for its benefits to people is debated by economists, as is its value in itself.
Nature also inspires industrial design: the field of biomimetics copies natural models, as when humpback whale fin ridges inspired wind turbine blades.
Biodiversity is a source of food, medicines and industrial materials, and recreation and tourism also rely on it.
The WWF's 2018 Living Planet Report argued that the whole global economy of US$125 trillion ultimately relies on nature.

contested_note: Economists debate whether biodiversity should be valued only for its benefits to people and whether money values for it are reliable.
notes: WWF figure appears in two framings: 3d5bd6bb2875 says the global economy of US$125 trillion relies on nature; ce58b0665949 says ecosystem services are worth US$125 trillion a year. Natural Asset Company 76579c189e5e calls $125 trillion a yearly funding gap. Verify which is right.

definition.text: Agricultural biodiversity is all the parts of biodiversity that matter for food and farming, the origin of every crop and farm animal.

facts.text: It earns income through food and raw materials and through services farms need, such as pollination, pest control, nutrient cycling and climate regulation.
Around 25% of the world's people are estimated to work in agriculture.
Putting a money value on biodiversity in farming and wild food is both hard and controversial.
By 2006 over 3 billion people depended on marine and coastal biodiversity for their livelihoods.

definition.text: Biological pest control uses natural enemies to keep pests down, an ecosystem function that depends on biodiversity.

facts.text: Control species can cut crop losses without the harms of chemical pesticides, bringing economic benefits.
Introducing control species without enough research can backfire: cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles became an invasive species.

definition.text: Biodiversity is a source of medicines and of ecosystem services that protect health.

facts.text: Over 40% of pharmaceutical products come from nature, and 70% of all cancer drugs are natural or bioinspired products.
Over 60% of the world's population still relies on herbal medicine as its main healthcare.
Quinine from Cinchona bark and artemisinin from sweet wormwood are plant-derived antimalarials.

definition.text: Biodiversity earns money through recreation and tourism, such as hiking, fishing and wildlife watching, as a cultural ecosystem service.

facts.text: Tourism accounts for 10% of the global job market.
The global ecotourism market was estimated at US$216.49 billion in 2023.
Tourism also harms biodiversity through habitat destruction and pollution, which led to sustainable tourism.

definition.text: The illegal wildlife trade profits by selling products from wild animals and plants, including endangered species.

facts.text: The Zoological Society of London estimates it is worth $23 billion a year.
Demand comes partly from culture, such as bushmeat and traditional medicine, while criminal and terrorist groups use trafficking to raise money.
It drives population declines, extinctions, loss of genetic diversity and the spread of disease and alien species.

title: Economic drivers of biodiversity loss
article: Economics of biodiversity#Impact of economic activity on biodiversity

definition.text: Economic activities often harm biodiversity, and their profits mean they are usually favoured over conservation and restoration.

facts.text: Main causes include habitat loss, land-use change, pollution and overexploitation.
BCG estimates that over 90% of human drivers of biodiversity loss come from agriculture, infrastructure, fashion and energy.
The IUCN estimates that 79% of threatened species are affected by agriculture, infrastructure, energy and mining.
Failing to halt land biodiversity loss between 2000 and 2010 was estimated to cost the global economy $500 billion.
Continued loss raises long-term risks such as pandemics, floods and droughts.

definition.text: Impact investing puts money into companies, organisations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return.

facts.text: It aligns an investor's values with where capital goes, in fields such as renewable energy, education and microfinance.
It spans asset classes such as private equity, venture capital and debt, and can target returns from below-market to above-market.
The term was coined in 2005, and modern impact funds grew prominent soon after the Great Recession.
In 2024 about 3,907 organisations managed an estimated $1.571 trillion in impact assets, far smaller than the $78 trillion global equity market.
Research finds many impact investors accept expected returns 2-4 percentage points lower in exchange for measurable social impact.
The SDGs need an estimated $5-7 trillion of investment a year, mostly expected from private capital, and impact investors linked their funds to them.

definition.text: Mission investments are investments by foundations, from part or all of their endowment, that further their charitable goals while earning a return.

facts.text: Program-related investments are below-market or concessionary investments made mainly for charitable aims, such as recoverable grants and cheap loans.
For US private foundations, program-related investments count towards the required 5 percent annual payout.
Mission-related investments seek market-rate returns from mission-driven organisations while supporting the endowment's growth.

definition.text: Environmental investing is the branch of impact investing aimed at a measurable positive environmental effect alongside financial returns.

facts.text: It funds projects such as clean energy, public transport and sustainable water management.
It arose from the recognition that huge private sums are needed to tackle climate change.
By 2024 green bonds had reached about $700 billion of cumulative issuance, and all sustainability-related bonds nearly $8 trillion.

title: Natural Asset Company

definition.text: A Natural Asset Company is a corporation set up to hold and manage natural assets so that private investors can fund conservation and regenerative land use.

facts.text: Each company holds rights to land or sea areas such as forests, ranches, grasslands or marine areas, and is run to maximise their ecological value.
It reports yearly both ordinary financial statements and Ecological Performance Reports valuing ecosystem services such as carbon retention and freshwater.
The NYSE proposed listing them publicly in 2021 but withdrew the proposal in January 2024 amid political backlash.
Critics on the right fear locked-up public land and speculation; critics on the left doubt markets are a responsible way to steward nature.

contested_note: Critics on both left and right dispute whether natural asset companies are a sound way to manage nature.
notes: 76579c189e5e calls $125 trillion an annual 'funding gap', which conflicts with the WWF figure's meaning elsewhere; not used.

definition.text: In the United States, donating a qualifying conservation easement can earn the landowner federal income tax deductions and other tax breaks.

facts.text: The donation's value is the drop in the property's market value caused by the easement, set by a qualified appraiser.
To qualify the easement must be perpetual, held by a qualified public or nonprofit body, and serve a real conservation purpose.
Easements can also cut estate taxes, since heirs pay on farmland value rather than development value.
Some states give tax credits, and Colorado and Virginia let landowners sell them to others.

definition.text: Governments, nonprofits and donors often buy conservation easements outright, paying landowners directly.

facts.text: The US Farm Bill is a key funder; in 2014 it created the Agricultural Conservation Easement Program for farmland and wetlands.
States commonly fund conservation through real estate transfer taxes, bonds and lottery proceeds.
Many states and counties run programmes to buy agricultural easements that keep farmland from development.

definition.text: A debt-for-nature swap forgives part of a developing country's foreign debt in exchange for that country investing locally in conservation.

facts.text: Thomas Lovejoy of WWF proposed the idea in 1987, after the Latin American debt crisis cut indebted countries' ability to fund conservation.
The first swap, in 1987, let Conservation International buy US$650,000 of Bolivian debt for US$100,000 in return for conservation commitments.
Swaps work where default risk is high, so funders can buy debt well below face value; the government then pays in local currency for conservation.
Most swaps occur in tropical, species-rich countries with rapid deforestation and fairly stable political systems.
Since 1987 they have generated over US$1 billion for conservation in developing countries.
Swaps fell from about five a year in the late 1980s and early 1990s to about two a year after 2000, partly because commercial debt became pricier.
Swap experience shaped later tools such as conservation trust funds.

definition.text: Debt-for-nature swaps come in three kinds: commercial three-party swaps run by NGOs, bilateral swaps between two governments, and multilateral swaps among several.

facts.text: In a three-party swap an NGO buys debt from commercial banks on the secondary market and passes it to the debtor in return for conservation commitments.
In a bilateral swap a creditor country forgives part of another government's debt in exchange for environmental commitments.
Recorded three-party swaps raised nearly US$140 million and bilateral and multilateral swaps nearly US$900 million for conservation from 1987-2010.

title: Criticism of debt-for-nature swaps

definition.text: Critics argue that debt-for-nature swaps bring little real debt relief, send money to the wrong places and can harm local people.

facts.text: Debt relieved by swaps is under 1% of total external debt even in countries that use them often.
Early on, nearly three-quarters of swap funds went to Costa Rica, while Brazil, despite rapid deforestation, took little part.
Early swaps often overlooked people living on the land set aside, and some were labelled eco-colonialism.
Supporters, by contrast, describe swaps as deals in which every party benefits.

contested_note: Supporters call swaps a win for all parties, while critics say they give little debt relief, misdirect funds and can harm local people.

title: Environmental, social, and governance

definition.text: ESG is an investing approach that weighs a company's environmental, social and corporate governance record alongside its finances.

facts.text: The term came to prominence in the 2004 UN-backed report 'Who Cares Wins'.
By 2023 ESG represented more than US$30 trillion in assets under management.
Environmental issues it weighs, such as emissions, biodiversity and waste, often reflect externalities not handled by markets.
The social pillar covers effects on workers and communities, and the governance pillar covers how firms are directed and controlled, including ethics, corruption and tax.
ESG saw outflows for the first time in 2023, and many US funds have dropped ESG terms from their names amid greenwashing claims.
Critics cite poor data and standards, greenwashing and claims that big asset managers impose rules without democratic oversight.
A 2005 legal report for UNEP's finance initiative concluded that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably part of investors' fiduciary duty.

contested_note: Critics dispute ESG's data quality, its standards and its political legitimacy.

definition.text: Responsible investors steer money using several methods: positive selection, exclusion, engagement, activism and integration of ESG factors.

facts.text: Positive selection picks companies meeting ESG criteria or the best performers in each sector.
Exclusion removes sectors or firms from consideration on ESG grounds; integration adds ESG risks and opportunities to ordinary financial analysis.
Engagement and activism use shareholder dialogue and voting to push companies to change.
The best-known early case was the 1970s and 1980s disinvestment from South Africa over apartheid.
Screening brings its own risks, such as concentration in a few sectors.

title: ESG and financial performance
article: Environmental, social, and governance#Relationship between ESG and Corporate Valuation

definition.text: Economists disagree about whether attention to ESG raises or lowers a company's value and investors' returns.

facts.text: Milton Friedman argued that social responsibility harms a firm's financial performance.
A 2011 study found the '100 Best Companies to Work For' beat their peers' stock returns by 2-3% a year.
Some studies link ESG indicators to higher value, while others say overinvesting in ESG can hurt it.
Some research suggests an inverted-U shape, with an optimal level of ESG spending beyond which returns fall.

contested_note: Studies of ESG and company value give mixed results, from positive to negative to inverted-U.

title: ESG rating agencies
article: Environmental, social, and governance#ESG rating agencies

definition.text: ESG rating agencies score companies on their ESG performance and are the main information providers for ESG investing.

facts.text: Sustainalytics counted over 600 ESG-rating companies in 2018, but the market is concentrating through takeovers.
Risk raters measure how exposed a firm is to ESG risks, so a high score need not mean a strong positive effect on the world.
Each agency uses its own metrics and no industry-wide standard exists.

definition.text: The Equator Principles are a framework banks use to assess and manage environmental and social risk in project finance.

facts.text: Launched in 2003, they were based on International Finance Corporation policy frameworks.
By October 2019, 97 institutions in 37 countries had adopted them, covering most international project finance debt.
Adopting banks commit not to lend to projects whose borrowers cannot meet their social and environmental policies.

title: Principles for Responsible Investment
article: Environmental, social, and governance#Principles for Responsible Investment

definition.text: The Principles for Responsible Investment is a UN-backed framework, set up in 2005, to help investors analyse ESG issues and act as responsible owners.

facts.text: As of April 2019 it had over 2,350 signatories.

definition.text: A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits.

facts.text: Like ordinary bonds, they can be issued by governments, development banks or companies, which repay the bond plus interest.
Eligible projects include renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution control, sustainable land use, biodiversity, clean transport and climate adaptation.
The European Investment Bank issued a Climate Awareness Bond in 2007, and the World Bank issued the first labelled green bond in 2008.
Green bonds mobilised over $93 billion in 2016, still only around 1% of global bond issuance.
By 2024 cumulative green bond issuance had reached about $700 billion.
Legally they barely differ from ordinary bonds: green promises are often not written into the contract in a binding way.
The EU Green Bonds Regulation came into force on 21 December 2024, creating the 'European Green Bond'.
Critics question the green credentials of some bonds and issuers, as when the Climate Bonds Initiative refused to list a Repsol bond in 2017.

conflicts.text: Green bond issuance rose 92% to $92 billion from 2015 to 2016.
conflicts.note: The fact uses $93 billion for 2016 (fd8f786f6292); another sentence of the same page gives $92 billion.

definition.text: The Green Bond Principles are voluntary market guidance from the International Capital Market Association on how green bonds should be run.

facts.text: They recommend a defined use of proceeds, a process for choosing projects, managing the money and regular reporting, sometimes with external review.
These practices aim to reduce information gaps between issuers and investors and support accountability.

definition.text: The greenium is the lower yield, or pricing premium, that green bonds often carry because investors want them.

facts.text: Empirical studies find high demand gives green bonds lower yields than ordinary equivalents.
The primary-market greenium ranges from -85 to +213 basis points, while the secondary market averages -1 to -9 basis points.
Voluntary green labels with weak oversight leave room for greenwashing, which may lead investors to accept lower returns than for brown investments.

title: Blended finance

definition.text: Blended finance uses public development money and charitable funds strategically to draw private investment into developing countries.

facts.text: It mixes public and private funds in one deal, each party using its expertise in a complementary way.
It aims at the Sustainable Development Goals, which in 2017 estimates needed an extra $2.5 trillion a year in financing.
Philanthropic or concessional money takes the first losses, reassuring private investors that their principal is protected.
Each concessional dollar can attract several private dollars, often 3x to 10x; a $2 million first-loss layer drawing $10 million is a 5x multiplier.
The OECD's Development Assistance Committee adopted blended finance principles in 2018.
The OECD identified 180 blended finance funds and facilities with $60.2 billion invested across 111 developing countries.
Critics say it shifts profits to private, mostly Northern, investors while leaving risks with Southern governments, and that its complexity weakens transparency.
In nature conservation it is used to overcome risk, small deal sizes and transaction costs that deter private investors.

contested_note: Scholars and NGOs criticise blended finance for shifting profits to private investors and risks to poorer countries' governments.

definition.text: Development funders support private investors in blended deals through technical assistance, risk underwriting and market incentives.

facts.text: Technical assistance uses grants to build investees' capacity and lower transaction costs.
Guarantees, insurance and concessional tranches reduce risks such as currency swings, political instability and default.
Because concessional capital is catalytic rather than continuous, it can be recycled into new projects once investors gain confidence.

definition.text: Land trusts are nonprofit or fiduciary arrangements that own and manage land, and sometimes water.

facts.text: The three common types are real estate investment trusts, community land trusts for affordable housing, and conservation land trusts.
Land trusts date back at least to Roman times, but their clearest history begins in Henry VIII's England.
In Australia, Aboriginal land trusts hold freehold title to land on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

definition.text: A catastrophe bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors.

facts.text: If the named disaster happens, the principal goes to the sponsor to fund recovery; otherwise investors get it back at maturity plus interest.
They were first used in the mid-1990s after Hurricane Andrew and the Northridge earthquake.
Rising climate-related disaster risk has led governments and insurers to use them when reinsurance is unavailable or too costly.
Investors like them because returns are largely uncorrelated with stocks and ordinary bonds, aiding diversification.
Swiss Re estimated the market at $43.1 billion at the end of 2023, with a record $15.4 billion issued that year.
Most are rated below investment grade, B or BB, based on the probability a qualifying disaster triggers a loss.

definition.text: Catastrophe bonds pay out under different triggers: the insurer's actual losses, modelled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured event parameters.

facts.text: Triggers closer to the insurer's own losses protect it better; index and parametric triggers spare investors from the insurer's claims handling.
A trigger can apply per single event or to the sum of losses over a period, usually a year.
Example: with a $90 billion aggregate attachment, three $20 billion hurricanes and a $40 billion earthquake total $100 billion and trigger payout.

definition.text: A conservation land trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation.

facts.text: It may own land outright or buy an easement or development, mining or logging rights while the land stays private.
Land trusts rely on donations, grants and public programmes; landowners often donate easements or land itself.
Many depend on volunteers: in the 2005 US census, 54% of land trusts were all-volunteer.
The first, the Trustees of Reservations in Massachusetts, was founded in 1891; by 2021 the US had over 1,300.
Most work regionally, though global ones include The Nature Conservancy and the World Land Trust.
Local and regional US trusts protected almost 9.4 million acres by 2003, double the 1998 figure.

definition.text: Environmental finance is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature.

facts.text: It seeks to move business resources toward sustainable investments while keeping profits.
Richard Sandor proposed a course on emission markets in 1992 at the University of Chicago, later called Environmental Finance.
Inspired by the idea of social cost, Sandor focused on cap-and-trade along with taxes and subsidies.
Under cap-and-trade, a total emissions cap is set and firms receive permits they can buy or sell, rewarding cuts and penalising excess.
The Dow Jones Sustainability Index, launched in 1999, rates the ecological and social impact of stocks for investors.
Climate finance, a part of it, splits into mitigation finance, which cuts emissions, and adaptation finance; mitigation takes over 90% of climate spending.

definition.text: Official development assistance is the OECD's measure of foreign aid: money that rich countries' governments give to promote poorer countries' development and welfare.

facts.text: The OECD Development Assistance Committee adopted the concept in 1969.
Most is grants, but soft loans count if their grant element is at least 25%.
ODA was US$168 billion in 2019, of which US$152 billion came from DAC donors.
In 2019, 28% of all ODA was multilateral, pooled through bodies such as the EU, the World Bank's IDA and UN agencies.
In 2025 aid from DAC donors fell 23% after inflation, the biggest yearly drop on record.
Critics call it an untidy, somewhat arbitrary category that counts spending mainly benefiting donors, such as refugee costs at home.
It is a channel for international public conservation finance, through grants, concessional loans and technical help.

definition.text: The best-known aid target says rich countries should give 0.7% of their national income as official development assistance.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly formalised it on 24 October 1970; Sweden and the Netherlands first met it in 1974, and few others have since.
DAC donors as a group have given around 0.3-0.35% of their income since the 1970s.
In 2019 six countries met the target, and the UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of income in 2021.

title: Tied aid

definition.text: Tied aid is aid given on condition that the money is spent on goods from the donor country or a small group of countries.

facts.text: Its legitimacy has long been disputed within the OECD's aid committee, which has set targets to reduce it.
A review found that in 2009, 51% of contract value was spent in donor countries though donors reported only 14% of aid as tied.

contested_note: Donors have long disputed whether tying aid to their own exports is legitimate.

definition.text: Parametric, or index-based, insurance pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached.

facts.text: Ordinary indemnity insurance pays the assessed loss after an event; parametric insurance only checks that the trigger was passed, using weather services, sensors or satellites.
Its main benefit is fast payout, giving cash for recovery soon after a disaster, and lower transaction costs.
Its main drawback is basis risk: payouts follow parameters, so they may not cover the full damage.
Mexico's Quintana Roo insures a coral reef with a wind-triggered policy paying up to $3.8 million a year; Hurricane Delta in 2020 triggered an $850,000 payout.
Pooled schemes such as the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, set up in 2007, let countries buy cover more cheaply than alone.

title: Social finance

definition.text: Social finance is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return.

facts.text: Unlike philanthropy, it sustains itself by being profitable for investors rather than relying on donors.
It has no agreed definition but includes impact investing, socially responsible investing and lending to social enterprises.
It grew quickly after the 2008 financial crisis as investors sought ethical alternatives.
Critics argue it pulls capital from productive uses, while backers say it adds direct investment where charity is declining.
It struggles with low returns, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect by mainstream banks and poor access to retail investors.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether social finance adds value beyond corporate social responsibility or simply diverts capital.

title: Social impact bond

definition.text: A social impact bond is an outcomes-based contract in which private investors fund a public programme and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary bonds, they have no fixed return; payment depends on social outcomes.
The first, launched in the UK in 2010, funded prisoner rehabilitation at Peterborough Prison.
By 2022 there were 276 projects with $745m raised, used in 23 countries as of May 2023.
Backers say taxpayers pay only for success; critics say they displace other funding and are an expensive way to run programmes.

contested_note: Advocates say social impact bonds reward success, while critics say they displace funding and cost more.

definition.text: A sustainability bond is a bond whose money must fund a mix of green and social projects.

facts.text: Green, social and sustainability bonds differ in which project categories the money may go to; sustainability bonds must combine both.
The ICMA principles are the most widely accepted framework for issuing all three kinds.
Critics warn of greenwashing because no single definition says what makes a bond sustainable.

definition.text: A sustainability-linked bond is a bond whose terms, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets.

facts.text: Performance is tracked with key performance indicators measured against sustainability performance targets.
Unlike green, social or sustainability bonds, the money raised can be used for general purposes.
Italian utility Enel issued the first in September 2019, promising a 25 basis point penalty on its coupon if it missed its target.
Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020; over 85% were tied to environmental indicators, most often emissions cuts.

title: Trophy hunting

definition.text: Trophy hunting is hunting for sport in which parts of the killed animal, such as the head, horns or hide, are kept and displayed.

facts.text: Supporters argue it gives economic reasons to conserve wildlife areas: 'if it pays it stays'.
The IUCN recognises that well-managed trophy hunting can create strong incentives to conserve species and habitats outside protected areas.
After South Africa legalised white rhino hunting, landowners reintroduced the species and numbers rose from under one hundred to more than 11,000.
Poorly managed, it can distort age and sex structures, disrupt social groups and cause population declines.
A 2017 Economists at Large report found trophy hunting was under one percent of tourism revenue in eight African countries, and critics say little reaches local communities.

contested_note: Supporters say trophy hunting funds conservation, while opponents say it is immoral and brings little money to conservation or local people.

definition.text: A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable security: the issuer borrows money and promises to pay the holder interest and repay the principal.

facts.text: Interest is usually paid at fixed intervals, often every six months or every year.
Bonds fund borrowers' long-term investments, or for governments, current spending.
Bondholders are lenders while stockholders are owners; bondholders are repaid first if the company goes bankrupt.
Bonds usually have a fixed term, or maturity, unlike stocks; most last less than 30 years.
They are issued by governments, banks, companies and international institutions, and are mostly bought by institutions such as pension funds and insurers.
The coupon is the interest rate the issuer pays; it can be fixed or float with a reference rate.

definition.text: A bond's yield is the rate of return an investor earns from it.

facts.text: Current yield is the yearly interest divided by the bond's market price.
Yield to maturity estimates the total return from buying at today's price and holding to the end, counting the present value of all payments.
Yield and price move in opposite directions: when market interest rates rise, bond prices fall.

definition.text: Credit quality is how likely a bond's borrower is to pay the promised amounts on time rather than default.

facts.text: High-yield bonds are rated below investment grade by credit rating agencies.
Because they are riskier, investors expect a higher yield from them.

definition.text: Bonds are grouped by issuer, currency, term and the conditions attached to them.

facts.text: Government or treasury bonds are issued by national governments; the safest, risk-free bonds pay the lowest interest.
Bonds under five years are often called short, 5 to 15 years medium, and over 15 years long.
Fixed-rate bonds pay a constant coupon, while floating rate notes pay a coupon linked to a reference rate.
Convertible bonds can be swapped for the issuer's shares, mixing debt and equity.

definition.text: Return on investment is the ratio of the profit an investment earns to what it cost.

facts.text: A high return on investment means the gains compare well with the cost.
It is used to judge how efficient one investment is or to compare several, and the one with the highest return is usually chosen first.
A simple form is the gain from the investment minus its cost, divided by its cost.
Example: $10,000 invested plus $200 in fees, worth $12,500 after a year with $300 in dividends, gives an annual return.
It is not adjusted for time, so long-term investments need a discounted version using net present value.
Traditional ROI ignores the value and risks of natural and social capital because it leaves out environmental, social and governance performance.

definition.text: Return on integration widens return on investment to count the long-term environmental and social returns of an investment alongside financial ones.

facts.text: The social cost of carbon can be built in to capture the damage an investment's emissions do to society.
It supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, combining financial, environmental and social results in one balance sheet.
A related method, social return on investment, measures environmental and social value not shown in ordinary accounts.

definition.text: A fiduciary is a person trusted to look after money or other assets for someone else and to act only in that person's interest.

facts.text: Trustees, financial advisers and managers of pension funds and endowments are fiduciaries.
Under Delaware law, which governs most large US firms, directors owe duties of care, loyalty and good faith.
A fiduciary must not let personal interest conflict with duty, nor profit from the position without informed consent.

title: Fiduciary duty and ESG

definition.text: A debate over whether investors' legal duty to beneficiaries allows, or even requires, them to weigh environmental, social and governance issues.

facts.text: A 2015 report, 'Fiduciary Duty in the 21st Century', concluded that ignoring long-term value drivers including ESG is itself a failure of fiduciary duty.
In the United States, some question whether pension funds that weigh such factors break their duty to maximise returns.
A 2005 legal report for UNEP similarly found that weighing ESG issues was permissible and arguably required.
One US state pension board blocked fossil fuel divestment on fiduciary grounds, though a 2019 analysis found the divested fund would have earned more.

contested_note: Investors and lawyers dispute whether fiduciary duty is a barrier to considering ESG issues.

definition.text: Diversification is spreading money across different investments so that no single asset or risk can do too much harm.

facts.text: The proverb 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' sums it up: more risk of losing one egg, less of losing them all.
If prices do not move in perfect step, a diversified portfolio varies less than the average of its parts.
It narrows the range of outcomes: returns never beat the best single asset nor fall below the worst.
Holding just one stock is risky; a single stock can fall 50% in a year.
A 1977 study found 30 stocks gave almost the same risk reduction as 1,000, and even four gave most of it.
Market correlations tend to rise in crises, weakening diversification just when investors need it.

definition.text: Diversifiable risk comes from a single company and can be spread away; systematic, or market, risk affects all assets and cannot.

facts.text: Buying all S&P 500 stocks leaves only the risk of index moves, while one stock also carries company-specific risk.
The company-specific part shrinks as more stocks are held, which is why it is called diversifiable.

definition.text: Mixing assets can bring a portfolio's variance, a measure of risk, below that of even its least risky asset.

facts.text: With fraction q in asset X and 1-q in uncorrelated asset Y, portfolio variance is q²σx² + (1-q)²σy².
Variance is lowest at q = σy²/(σx²+σy²), giving σx²σy²/(σx²+σy²), below either asset held alone.
Markowitz's 1952 mean-variance framework showed portfolio risk depends on the covariance among returns, not just each asset's variance.

definition.text: Stock is all the shares into which ownership of a company is divided; one share is a fraction of ownership.

facts.text: A share usually entitles its holder to part of the company's earnings, part of what is left after debts in liquidation, and votes.
Common stock usually carries votes; preferred stock usually does not but gets dividends first.
Selling shares to the public on a stock exchange for the first time is an initial public offering, or IPO.
Raising money by selling stock is equity financing, while issuing bonds is debt financing that avoids giving up ownership.
A share's price at any moment is set by supply and demand for it.
Shareholders' claims on company assets rank below those of creditors.

definition.text: Eco-investing, or green investing, is socially responsible investing focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices.

facts.text: Unlike broader socially responsible investing, it narrows to environmental issues, especially renewable energy and clean technology.
One tracker estimated over $1.248 trillion invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007.
New green technologies carry high up-front costs that are harder to justify to investors.

title: Sustainable community

definition.text: A sustainable community is one planned, built or changed to promote sustainable living.

facts.text: Such communities focus on environmental and economic sustainability, infrastructure, social equity and local government.
The term's definition is contested and still under construction.

notes: Navbox page only loosely related to conservation finance (urban planning and local initiatives); excluded per scope brief.

title: Sustainability organization

definition.text: A sustainability organization is a group that works to advance sustainability, or the act of organising something sustainably.

facts.text: For such organisations, sustainability can be an end in itself rather than a route to economic benefit.
Corporate sustainability means a company voluntarily including social and environmental concerns in its operations.

notes: Navbox page that is mostly a list of organisations; not a finance concept. Excluded per scope brief.

title: Blue bond

definition.text: A blue bond is the ocean version of a green bond: it raises money specifically for ocean conservation and sustainable marine activity.

facts.text: Like green bonds, blue bonds earmark money for eligible environmental projects and usually follow voluntary guidance on use of proceeds, project selection, management and reporting.
Labelled bonds tied to sustainable fisheries, such as the Seychelles sovereign blue bond, are discussed as a way to bring private capital to nature.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; frame lists 'Seychelles Blue Bond' elsewhere.

definition.text: An obligation to repay money borrowed or otherwise owed to another party.

facts.text: Debt can be owed by a country, local government, company or individual; loans, bonds, notes and mortgages are all forms of it.
Repayment may be structured as the whole principal due at maturity, amortized over the loan term, or partly amortized with the rest due at the end.
A debt is secured if creditors can claim specific collateral; unsecured debt gives creditors no recourse to the borrower's assets.
Governments issue debt for ongoing expenses and capital projects; their overall indebtedness is usually shown as a debt-to-GDP ratio.
Rating agencies such as Moody's, Standard & Poor's and Fitch grade government and corporate debt by the debtor's ability to honour it.
Bonds are tradeable debt securities, while loans are not securities, though securitization can turn loans into them.
Debt is denominated in a currency, so inflation or deflation can change its effective size even when borrower and lender use the same currency.

definition.text: The reduction of an asset, or the sale of a business, for financial, ethical or political objectives.

facts.text: Firms divest to focus on core operations, raise cash, stabilise results, drop failing units, or comply with regulators; shareholder pressure for social reasons is often called disinvestment.
Divestment for social goals includes campaigns over apartheid South Africa, tobacco, factory farming, and fossil fuels, the last coordinated by 350.org since the 2010s.
As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions holding over $40.5 trillion had begun or committed to some fossil fuel divestment.
Financial research suggests fossil fuel divestment has raised investors' returns in the longer term.
